habits.title: My Habits
habits.start_journey: Start your journey by creating your first habit
habits.guide_subtitle: A concise guide to building lasting habits

guide_content.intro_p1: Habits are the invisible foundation of success. They are not just repeated actions; they are what our brain automates to save energy. Improving by 1% each day can lead to significant long‑term change.
guide_content.intro_p2: The secret is not just setting goals, but creating a habit system consistent with the person you want to become.
guide_content.identity_p1: Many fail to change not because they "don't care enough", but because they focus only on outcomes.
guide_content.identity_p2: The three layers of behavior change are: Outcomes (what you get), Processes (what you do), Identity (what you believe). Real change starts from identity — decide who you want to be, then prove it to yourself with small wins.
guide_content.understanding_p1: Every habit follows a loop called the feedback loop:
guide_content.understanding_craving_desc: the motivation to perform the action
guide_content.laws_title: The Four Laws of Behavior Change
law1_items: Use implementation intentions: "I will [behavior] at [time] in [place]"
Use habit stacking: "After [current habit], I will [new habit]"
Design your environment — make cues visible
law2_items: Use temptation bundling: pair a needed habit with a desired one
Join a culture where the desired behavior is the norm
Create a motivation ritual before a difficult habit
law3_items: Reduce friction — decrease the steps between you and good habits
Use the Two‑Minute Rule: start with just 2 minutes
Automate habits using technology when possible
law4_items: Use reinforcement — give yourself an immediate reward
Use a habit tracker — "don't break the chain"
Never miss twice — get back on track quickly
advanced_items: The Goldilocks Rule: stay motivated by working on tasks of manageable difficulty
The downside of good habits: don't let them run on autopilot — keep reviewing and improving them
Genes don't determine destiny; they determine areas of opportunity. Choose habits that fit your natural strengths.
guide_content.final_p1: Success is not a goal to reach. It is a system to build.
guide_content.final_p2: Small changes. Remarkable results. One habit at a time.

challenges.guide_title: How to Master Breaking Bad Habits
challenges.guide_subtitle: A guide to letting go of what harms you

guide_content.intro_p1: Breaking a bad habit is not about willpower — it's about strategy. Your brain has automated these behaviors, and the only way to change them is to understand how they work and interrupt the pattern.
guide_content.intro_p2: This guide will help you apply the science of behavior change to eliminate habits that no longer serve you.
guide_content.why_p1: Bad habits provide immediate gratification while consequences are delayed. Your brain prioritizes instant rewards, making it hard to resist.
guide_content.why_p2: Understanding the habit loop (Cue → Craving → Response → Reward) is the first step to breaking free.
guide_content.inversion_intro: To break a bad habit, invert the four laws of behavior change:
inv1_items: Stop following accounts that promote the behavior
Change your routine to avoid cue exposure
inv2_items: Highlight the true costs of the behavior
Reframe your identity: "I'm not someone who does this"
Associate the habit with negative outcomes
inv3_items: Add friction between you and the bad habit
inv4_items: Create an accountability partner or system
Use a habit scorecard to track slip‑ups
guide_content.replacement_p1: The most effective strategy is not just to stop — it's to replace. When you feel the urge, redirect toward a healthier alternative that satisfies the same need.
replacement_items: Bored? → Do a quick workout or creative activity
Stressed? → Try deep breathing or journaling
Lonely? → Call a friend or join a community
guide_content.mindset_p1: Don't focus on what you're giving up. Focus on what you're gaining: freedom, clarity, self‑respect, and a life aligned with your values.
guide_content.mindset_p2: Every moment of resistance is building the person you want to become.
guide_content.final_p1: You don't need to be perfect. You need to be consistent.
guide_content.final_p2: Break the pattern. Build the life you deserve.

understanding_section.title: Understanding the Problem
understanding_section.description: Modern online pornography is designed to hijack your brain's reward system. Understanding the science behind it is the first step to freedom.
understanding_section.super_stimulus_intro_part2: — an artificially enhanced version of a natural reward that your brain never evolved to handle:
understanding_section.unlimited_novelty_desc: Infinite content triggers dopamine spikes far beyond what natural experiences provide
understanding_section.instant_access_desc: No effort required means no natural delay between desire and reward
understanding_section.extreme_content_desc: Increasingly extreme material pushes your brain's reward threshold ever higher
understanding_section.super_stimulus_conclusion: Your brain releases more dopamine anticipating and seeking than during the actual experience, creating a powerful cycle of craving.
understanding_section.desensitization_desc: Your brain becomes less responsive to dopamine, requiring more intense stimulation to feel the same pleasure.
understanding_section.escalation_desc: Over time, you may seek more extreme or novel content to get the same effect.
understanding_section.anxiety_desc: The cycle of use and remorse can fuel anxiety, shame, and negative self‑perception.
understanding_section.concentration_desc: Dopamine dysregulation affects focus, motivation, and the ability to enjoy everyday activities.
understanding_section.pied_desc: Many men experience difficulty with arousal during real intimate encounters. This happens because the brain has been conditioned to respond only to artificial porn stimulation, not real partners.
understanding_section.emotional_disconnection_desc: Regular porn use can make it harder to form deep emotional bonds. Real intimacy requires vulnerability and connection that porn trains you to bypass.

understanding_section.young_brains_intro_part2: — the brain's high capacity to form new neural pathways.

understanding_section.young_brains_point3: Neural pathways formed during this period become deeply ingrained
understanding_section.young_brains_point4: Early exposure can shape lifelong sexual arousal patterns
understanding_section.good_news_desc: The same neuroplasticity that makes young brains vulnerable also means they can rewire faster during recovery.

brain_science_section.wanting_desc: It's the anticipation, the seeking, the drive. Dopamine pushes you to seek the reward, not to enjoy it. That's why you can spend hours searching and clicking, feeling unsatisfied.
brain_science_section.liking_desc: Real satisfaction and enjoyment. With porn, this system weakens — you want more but enjoy it less. Real pleasures appear dull by comparison.
brain_science_section.wanting_liking_quote: "The gap between wanting and liking is the trap. You're chasing a satisfaction that never arrives."
brain_science_section.novelty_desc_part1: Your brain is wired to pay attention to
brain_science_section.novelty_desc_part2: Each new image or video triggers a dopamine spike because your brain thinks: "This might be important!"

brain_science_section.escalation_step2: Same content → Less dopamine → Need for more novelty
brain_science_section.escalation_step3: Seek more extreme/new content → Higher spike → Tolerance builds

brain_science_section.novelty_conclusion: This is why many users find themselves watching content they never would have sought at the start. It's not about what you want — it's about what your hijacked reward system demands.

dopamine.title: How Dopamine Works
dopamine.summary: Understand the brain's reward system and why recovery takes time.
content: Dopamine is a neurotransmitter that plays a crucial role in how we experience pleasure and motivation. It's often called the 'feel‑good' chemical, but it's more accurately described as the 'seeking' chemical.

When we engage in addictive behaviors, our brain releases unusually high amounts of dopamine. Over time, the brain adapts by reducing dopamine receptors, which means we need more stimulation to feel the same pleasure.

During recovery, your brain is literally rewiring itself. Dopamine receptors are regenerating and your baseline sense of pleasure is recalibrating. This process takes time — typically 90‑180 days for significant improvement.
The good news: your brain has remarkable plasticity. Every day of recovery, you are building new neural pathways and restoring healthy dopamine function.
key_takeaways: Dopamine drives seeking behavior, not just pleasure
Recovery involves physical changes in the brain
90‑180 days for significant receptor regeneration
Your brain can and will heal

relapses.title: Managing Relapses
relapses.summary: Relapses aren't failures — they're learning opportunities. Here's how to handle them.
content: First, let's reframe relapse: it's not a moral failure nor a sign that recovery isn't working. Relapse is often part of the recovery process, and research shows that most people who successfully recover experience multiple relapses.
The key is how you respond. The abstinence violation effect is when a slip leads to completely abandoning recovery efforts. Avoiding this mindset is crucial.
After a relapse: 1) Don't catastrophize — one slip doesn't erase your progress. 2) Analyze what triggered it. 3) Identify what you could do differently. 4) Get right back on track. 5) Seek support.

Prevention strategies include: identifying your triggers, creating environmental barriers, having an accountability partner, and building healthy sources of dopamine through exercise, social connection, and meaningful goals.
key_takeaways: Relapse is often part of recovery, not its end
One slip doesn't erase all progress
Analyze triggers and learn from each experience
Get back on track immediately — don't wait for 'tomorrow'

withdrawal.title: Understanding Withdrawal
withdrawal.summary: What to expect during withdrawal and how to cope.
content: Withdrawal symptoms are the brain's response to the absence of the high dopamine levels it had become accustomed to. Common symptoms include: irritability, anxiety, depression, difficulty concentrating, insomnia, and intense cravings.
The acute phase (first 1‑2 weeks) is typically the most challenging. Symptoms peak around days 3‑7 and gradually subside. Understanding this timeline helps you know the worst is temporary.

Management strategies: stay hydrated, exercise regularly (even light walks help), maintain a sleep schedule, avoid isolation, use breathing exercises during craving peaks, and remember that every difficult moment is your brain healing.
Physical activity is especially powerful — it naturally boosts dopamine and endorphins, helping bridge the neurochemical gap left during recovery.
key_takeaways: Symptoms peak in the first week, then improve
Exercise is one of the best management tools
Every difficult moment is literally healing your brain
Stay connected — don't isolate

habits.title: Building New Habits
habits.summary: Replace old patterns with healthy routines that last.
content: Breaking an addiction isn't just about stopping a behavior — it's about replacing it with something better. Your brain craves the reward pathway the addiction provided, so you need to build new pathways.

The habit loop consists of: Cue → Routine → Reward. To change a habit, identify your cues (time, place, emotional state), replace the routine with a healthier one, and make sure you still get a reward.
Start small. Trying to overhaul your entire life at once leads to burnout. Focus on one keystone habit — often exercise — that creates positive ripple effects on sleep, mood, and motivation.
Consistency beats intensity. A daily 10‑minute walk is more powerful than an occasional hour‑long workout. Habits are built through repetition, not intensity.
key_takeaways: Replace, don't just eliminate — fill the void
Identify your cues and plan alternative responses
Start with one keystone habit
Consistency beats intensity every time

neuroplasticity.title: Your Brain Can Change
neuroplasticity.summary: The science of neuroplasticity and why recovery is always possible.
content: Neuroplasticity is the brain's ability to reorganize itself by forming new neural connections. This means that no matter how long you've struggled, your brain can change and heal.

Every time you resist an urge, you are strengthening new neural pathways. It's like building a muscle — each repetition makes the next one slightly easier. The brain literally changes its structure based on your choices.

Studies show that meditation, exercise, and learning new skills accelerate neuroplasticity. These activities increase BDNF (brain‑derived neurotrophic factor), which helps create new neurons and connections.

The timeline for noticeable changes varies, but most people report significant improvements in clarity, mood, and cravings between 30‑90 days. Remember: you're not just waiting for change — you're actively building it.
key_takeaways: Your brain can physically change at any age
Every healthy choice strengthens recovery pathways
Exercise and meditation speed up brain healing
30‑90 days typically bring noticeable improvements
